channel.title: Security + Policy + Governance News Aggregator
channel.description: Curated Security, Cybersecurity Policy, and Governance news from trusted international sources

item.title: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
item.description: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.

item.title: 354 dark web vendors and buyers arrested in Europol-coordinated global crackdown
item.description: Europol, in collaboration with law enforcement agencies from 14 countries across the globe, have successfully identified vendors and buyers from major dark marketplaces as part of Operation TorNado, a coordinated international effort targeting cybercrime, drug trafficking, and firearms offences. The operation, which spanned from May 2025 to October 2026, resulted in 354 arrests and hundreds of house searches worldwide.

item.title: Keeping pace with e-evidence: New report examines Europe’s digital forensic capabilities
item.description: Coordinated by the European Commission in cooperation with Europol, the analysis draws on stakeholder consultations, dedicated meetings, surveys and contributions from experts at Europol’s European Cybercrime Centre.The findings point to common challenges: investigative tools, resources and expertise are struggling to keep pace with the forms and volume of digital evidence created by modern technologiesDigitalisation shaping evidence landscapeDigital information is spread...

item.title: 5th EMPACT Hackathon leads to the detection of 51 potential victims
item.description: An international operation involving 40 experts and investigators from 20 countries has identified 51 potential victims of human trafficking, as well as five suspects. Held in Amsterdam from 23 to 25 September 2026, the fifth EMPACT Hackathon against the digital aspects of human trafficking brought together police officers, labour authorities and specialists in online investigations, supported by Europol and Eurojust.

item.title: Investment scams with potential victims in at least 50 countries: over 100 servers seized
item.description: Led by the German Itzehoe Public Prosecutor's Office (Staatsanwaltschaft Itzehoe), the operation targeted a company suspected of supplying fraudulent trading websites to criminal groups. The entity is connected to call centre operators who allegedly persuaded victims to hand over their savings. Investigators estimate losses exceeding EUR 4 million.Authorities searched 17 locations and seized servers, other evidence and assets. Seven suspects...

item.title: Five TEFAF robbery suspects added to EU Most Wanted
item.description: As of 29 October 2026, five new fugitives, four men and one woman, have been added to the EU Most Wanted list. According to the Limburg Public Prosecutor's Office (Openbaar Ministerie) and the Dutch Police (Politie), all five suspects are involved in the European Fine Art Fair (TEFAF) robbery that took place on 28 June 2022 in Maastricht, the Netherlands.

item.title: SAP security advisory – November 2026 monthly rollup (AV26-1137)
27 arrests and 248 potential victims identified in action week against labour exploitation
item.description: Europol, the European Labour Authority (ELA), and 34 participating countries today announced the results of an action week targeting human trafficking for labour exploitation. The operation, part of an EMPACT action led by Sweden, brought together police, border guards, labour and social security inspectorates, and tax authorities to crack down on exploitative practices in high-risk sectors such as agriculture, construction, cosmetic services, massage parlours, and hospitality.

item.title: Microsoft security advisory – November 2026 monthly rollup (AV26-1142) – Update 1
Google and Anthropic push for faster patches as AI collapses bug discovery timelines
item.description:
AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has made it untenable for software vendors to sit on privately reported flaws for months, and Google Project Zero is responding by shrinking its vulnerability disclosure deadline from 90 to 60 days, with plans to drop it to 30 days a year from now. Anthropic is following suit with an even more aggressive timeline.

Project Zero is Google’s elite vulnerability research team that regularly reports vulnerabilities in widely used open-source and proprietary software, much of which is critical to internet infrastructure. Its 90-day deadline for vendors to produce patches before the team releases vulnerability details publicly was a major stake in the ground for the security research community when it was announced in 2014, and it has become the de facto standard for coordinated disclosure.

The team’s announcement Friday that it will reduce this deadline to 60 days starting in February and 30 days starting in January 2028 is important because when Project Zero speaks, the security industry listens. And it did. On Monday, Anthropic announced it will adjust its disclosure policy from 90 days to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues, and to 45 days for all other issues, starting in January. Other security companies and researchers will likely follow.

The rationale is explicitly due to the offensive cyber capabilities of large language models: not only in discovering new vulnerabilities, but in reverse engineering patches and using them as blueprints for finding additional flaws in the same code.

“LLMs have increased the speed at which attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities, alongside the risk that multiple parties, including malicious ones, discover the same bug,” Project Zero researcher Natalie Silvanovich said in a blog post. “A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster.”

Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team said essentially the same: “A 90-day window made sense when a vulnerability could be expected to stay private for months. We no longer believe it can, and these changes are intended to keep pace with progress in AI capabilities and strike the right balance for defenders.”

‘Soak time’ has become meaningless

Since 2021, Project Zero’s policy has actually been “90+30” with 90 days to develop a patch, plus 30 days of grace while the patch rolled out to users. The team referred to these extra 30 days as “soak time.”

But in a world where AI agents can analyze patches to determine flaw details in minutes and then write exploits for them, waiting for a patch to propagate before releasing vulnerability details only creates a false sense of secrecy. As a result, the Project Zero’s previous 30-day grace is gone effective immediately.

In a report published this week, Google’s Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) documented the first fully automated AI-powered vulnerability discovery-and-exploitation pipeline it has observed in the wild. Called exploit_agent, the framework is designed to analyze application code changes following security patches, identify vulnerabilities, and generate exploits without requiring an operator to direct each step.

While Anthropic has different deadlines based on vulnerability severity, Project Zero decided to abandon severity as a disclosure metric because attackers are just as likely to discover low-risk flaws as they are to find the high-risk ones.

“When vendors determine severity and use it to prioritize bug fixes, they are making decisions about what risks they are willing to expose their users to, and it is reasonable to accept the risk of low-severity bugs, like unexploitable null pointer crashes or minor info leaks in a lot of circumstances,” Project Zero’s Silvanovich said. “But this doesn’t change the availability of these vulnerabilities to attackers, and we want our policy to reflect this reality.”

Google’s team will also no longer check whether a vendor’s patch fixes the issue when deciding whether to release details or not, because this back-and-forth can quickly become unmanageable, especially because the team now finds vulnerabilities using AI assistance at a much faster pace and because vendors might choose alternative mitigation strategies such as temporarily disabling a vulnerable feature or code path until a full patch can be developed.

“We decided on a policy that encourages vendors to improve remediation time on a schedule that is challenging but realistic, with the hope that this will lead to vendors broadly improving their remediation processes and infrastructure in a way that eventually enables them to fix all reported vulnerabilities quickly,” Silvanovich said.

The road ahead will be bumpy for users

The shorter patch deadlines come at a time when open-source projects and software vendors are already drowning in vulnerability reports and must resort to either AI-assisted patching or hiring more developers, if they can afford it. As of last week, the number of CVEs issued this year exceeded 100,000, more than double last year’s count.

Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team noted that “models can now help develop fixes” as one justification for the more aggressive disclosure deadlines, and said it will include “actionable guidance with each report, along with a patch or mitigation where possible,” to help maintainers confirm flaws and fix them.

However, multiple studies and developers have reported in recent months that AI-generated patches are often incomplete, failing to address the root causes of a flaw, to eliminate all instances of the bug from the codebase, or to block all exploit variations.

Security firm XOR built a benchmark that pitted frontier coding systems against vulnerabilities the company had discovered in a private software stack. No public fix existed for any of the flaws when the evaluation ran, so the systems had to work from the vulnerable code alone. The best models produced complete fixes for only about a third of the flaws: 35.3% for GPT-6 Astra and 28.6% for Claude Fable 5.1. Across all systems, just 11.9% of patch attempts earned full credit.

According to an analysis by VulnCheck, seven months after launching its Mythos-powered Glasswing vulnerability-hunting program, Anthropic’s public ledger counts 37,966 findings, but only 217 of the 7,349 flaws made public so far have been fixed.

Project Zero acknowledges the friction between the need to patch faster and devs being overloaded. The team solicited feedback from the vendors it reports to most and chose the phased schedule because an immediate change could push vendors to stop trying to meet the disclosure deadlines.

“To respond to these new timelines, organizations should be better prepared to assess whether compensating controls can reduce the risk of a vulnerability when it’s disclosed,” Ramy Rahman, senior principal solutions engineer at ArmorCode, tells CSO. “With disclosures arriving sooner, and sometimes before a fix is available, teams need a process for evaluating exposure, applying available mitigations, and tracking remediation.”

“Consider hardening systems at deployment time and removing software you don’t use,” he said. “Leaner, more deliberate deployments can reduce exposure and make vulnerability findings easier to manage.”

item.title: Optimizely confirms massive cyberattack on customer websites injected stealer malware
item.description:
Attackers apparently from China used an authentication security hole within the popular Optimizely AI platform for marketers to steal from at least 178 sites owned by some of the planet’s largest companies. 

Named victims featured vendors including Zoom, Paychex, Equifax, and GitLab, and end-user enterprises including Starbucks, IKEA, Mattel, American Eagle, Air France, Mutual of Omaha, Heineken, Home Chef, Cinnabon, American Eagle, Levi, Costco and HSBC.

Salesforce issued a statement confirming that it had also been impacted by the attack.

“Salesforce is investigating unauthorized modifications to scripts provided by Optimizely and used on certain Salesforce websites,” it wrote in an email statement. “As a precaution, Salesforce is confirming that Optimizely scripts are disabled across preview and production instances.”

The attacks were discovered by UK-based security researcher Scott Helme, the founder of Report URI, who said in an interview that his team had confirmed 178 victims, but that there could be more. “That’s the number that we directly observed and that all carried the same infection,” he said. 

Helme published a report about the attacks on Monday, in which he described an attack methodology where an Optimizely capability in its Web Experimentation product facilitating adding members to a site’s development team was leveraged to insert malware into the sites.

“The malware was a multi-purpose kit. It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker’s, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and on iPhones and iPads it delivered the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits,” Helme wrote. “The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy. A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.” 

Optimizely customers load a JavaScript “snippet” from Optimizely’s CDN onto their sites which contains Optimizely code, the customer’s A/B tests, and an optional field called Project JavaScript containing custom code written by the customer. The report said that attackers inserted their own code into the customer’s Project JavaScript and left the rest of each snippet untouched. “The file was still served from cdn[.]Optimizely[.]com, with Optimizely’s certificate, from a host that every affected site already trusted,” it noted.

The report described how the observed attack worked. “The script watches form submissions and every fetch/XHR POST for a card number, expiry date and CVV,” it said. “When it has all three, it sends them to https://1688360[.]cc/card[.]php with navigator.sendBeacon. Cards entered in hosted payment iframes [such as] Stripe, Adyen and similar were out of its reach. Cards typed into a site’s own form fields were not.”

Analyst questions the claims of a fix

Optimizely, which did not reply to an interview request, confirmed the attacks on its site. In an email shared with customers, Optimizely said that attackers “exploited a vulnerability in the Experimentation account signup flow. They used it to impersonate a user and add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. We have blocked access to the vulnerable path and deployed a fix.”

The email also said that the company had “ended active sessions and revoked tokens and reset access for affected user accounts” and that it also had “removed the injected code from affected projects” and “blocked any code from being delivered in Cloudflare.”

The company used highly confident wording to describe its fix, saying that “the Optimizely Experimentation platform is fully secured” and that “modification of Javascript no longer possible.”  

Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, raised an eyebrow at those claims.

To begin with, he noted a discrepancy in the timelines published by the vendor and the security researcher. “Optimizely puts the first malicious write at 07:51. Report URI saw the BBC’s Optimizely snippet loading attacker code at 04:21, three and a half hours earlier,” he said. “The forensics report should reconcile that gap. Customers need the real start time to scope their exposure.”

As well, he pointed out, “Optimizely seems very comfortable stating absolutes early in a forensics investigation. Those are verdicts from a company whose forensics are still underway and whose timeline disagrees with outside research.”

No responsibility for the attack claimed

Helme speculated in an interview that the attackers were a small group of thieves, almost certainly coming from China, noting that he saw extensive Chinese writing in the code and that the attacks “tie back to infrastructure that has been used by other Chinese actors.”

“They are either Chinese or they really want us to think that they are Chinese,” Helme said, adding that the nature of what was stolen makes it highly unlikely the attackers were state actors. State actors, he said, would likely have used the malware on major news sites to create and spread false stories. 

Asked if his team could verify Optimizely’s claim that it had fixed the hole, he said that he couldn’t yet. Some of the infected sites were cleaned up, but he has to wait to see if they get reinfected before concluding that the original hole had been closed. 

Recommendation to customers ‘concerning’

Dickson said that one line in Optimizely’s email to customers was especially concerning.

“Optimizely’s documentation tells customers to allow ‘unsafe-eval‘ in their policy. At HSBC, the policy blocked the main payload and the data theft, but a backup copy of the malicious code ran anyway through that setting. A vendor’s setup guide should not quietly loosen its customers’ defenses,” Dickson said. “Restrict script-src to the hosts a page actually needs. Lock down connect-src so stolen data has nowhere to go. Drop ‘unsafe-eval‘ wherever possible. Start in report-only mode so nothing breaks.”

He added, “the Optimizely attack may be about as bad as a third-party script compromise gets. Optimizely owes its customers a clear explanation of how one flaw reached so many unrelated companies.”

item.title: How organizations can secure their AI-generated code
item.description:
The IT manager didn’t know the company hired a “vibe coder” straight out of school. By the time they met a few months later, the new hire had already built a web application that operated with customer data and private contracts.

The app ran under a domain the new hire controlled, stored data on Supabase’s free plan, and deployed directly from his GitHub repository to Cloudflare’s serverless infrastructure.

“He vibe-codes everything straight into production, on servers all over the world,” the IT manager wrote on Reddit. “We’re EU based.”

When asked whether he had read the AI-generated code or taken any security precautions, the new hire said, “My GitHub repo is private.”

The IT manager took the concern to the CEO, who brushed it aside: “Let it go.”

In many organizations, vibe coders build software without thinking much about security. Their apps may get the job done, but they are ticking bombs.

In SusVibes, a benchmark of 186 real-world feature requests from open-source projects, agents given feature descriptions without security guidance produced working code up to 57% of the time. But only 11.8% of their solutions were secure.

“The failures we saw were not careless errors,” says Danqing Wang of Carnegie Mellon University’s Language Technologies Institute, author of the paper describing SusVibes. “Spotting those requires reasoning about what an attacker can do, not just what the feature should do.”

What has changed, especially this year, is that AI code-generating tools have gotten so good at producing working code that people are just trusting them, says Dr. Katie Paxton-Fear, staff security advocate at Semgrep. “Developers simply aren’t being as critical now as they were when AI was worse at writing code.”

Whether it’s the vibe-coder in marketing or the seasoned engineering team boosting its productivity, AI-generated code is an increasing security concern for CISOs. Much of that is a function of volume, but even as AI has proved highly capable of finding flaws in code bases, it is not yet adept at contributing code without introducing its own.

Treating AI-generated code as ‘untrusted input’

Leading AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and Amazon Q Developer have become developer go-to tools, and CIOs are increasingly enlisting business users to vibe code their own apps.

But as AI-generated code surfaces everywhere, CISOs have only one option: to treat it “as untrusted input that has to earn its way into the codebase,” says Bianca Lankford, VP of engineering at Datadog.

To do so, security leaders are moving security checks closer to where code is written: static analysis, secrets scanning, and dependency checks run on every pull request and, increasingly, in the developer’s editor.

“Companies are also approving specific AI tools, limiting what assistants can access, and training reviewers to spot common AI mistakes like outdated libraries, weak input validation, and overly permissive defaults,” Lankford adds.

At Mimecast, using AI to write code doesn’t remove the developer’s responsibility for it, says Leslie Nielson, CISO at the information security vendor. “A named person owns every AI-assisted change that ships, and that’s recorded in the pull request, not assumed,” he adds. “AI can propose. Only people can approve.”

The volume of code organizations need to review is only growing, and reviewing everything manually can be impossible. That’s why Nielsen recommends security leaders combine automated checks with human judgment.

“We use automation for the known and repetitive, like dependency checks, secrets detection, and standard vulnerability patterns,” he says. “We keep a person accountable for anything involving access, authentication, or sensitive data. Those categories always go to a specialist reviewer, regardless of how clean the scan looks.”

Datadog’s Lankford says the decision to bring in a specialist should depend on what the code could put at risk, not on what entity — human or AI — wrote it. “Anything involving authentication, cryptography, payments, personal data, or infrastructure goes to a specialist, and code owner rules can route those changes automatically,” she says. “Other useful signals include diff size, new dependencies, and changes to permissions or network exposure.”

The goal is to protect the human reviewers’ attention. “A reviewer buried in low-risk changes isn’t reviewing,” Nielsen adds. “They’re approving.”

Another priority should be preserving the knowledge behind the code. “Generative AI may produce software, but it cannot produce understanding,” notes Alex Ștefănescu, security expert and tech activist. “Documentation, a solid test suite, and a written record of every significant architecture decision ever made are going to save developers and organizations countless hours when a security incident hits or when they are debugging complex issues.”

All of this should be created and maintained by people and intended for human use, not externalized to generative algorithms, Ștefănescu adds.

What’s at risk with AI-generated code

The inclusion of third-party libraries or phantom dependencies — dependencies that are not explicitly declared in a manifest file — is a common concern with AI-generated code, as these unreported software packages might not be identified during a scan and can potentially hide vulnerabilities. 

One way to address this is to use software composition analysis (SCA) and software supply chain security tools to help identify the libraries in use, as well as the vulnerabilities and potential legal and compliance issues that might bring. 

While not unique to AI-generated code, organizations also expose themselves to risks when developers download machine learning (ML) models or datasets from platforms such as Hugging Face. 

“In spite of security checks on both ends, it may still happen that the model contains a backdoor that becomes active once the model is integrated,” says Ștefănescu. “This could ultimately lead to data being leaked from the company that used the malicious models.”

When it comes to coding agents and code completion functionality in tools like GitHub Copilot, Ștefănescu worries about hallucinations. “An LLM will always generate the most statistically probable continuation of a given prompt, so there are no real guarantees in place that it will generate a real package from PyPI, for example, after the word ‘import’,” they say. “Some attackers are aware of this and register package names on platforms like npm and PyPI, filling in some functionality that code completion tools suggest in order to make the packages seem legitimate.”

If these packages are imported into real applications, they can do real damage.

Sensitive information inadvertently leaking into codebases because of developers using AI-powered coding tools is another key concern.

To address these risks, CISOs can establish protocols for downloading and integrating ML models or datasets from external platforms such as Hugging Face and ensure those protocols are incorporated in AI code agents’ instruction files where applicable. Such protocols can include implementing automated scanning tools to detect malicious code or backdoors, having a policy that only allows the use of models from verified publishers, or conducting internal testing in isolated environments.

Not all AI-based code comes from teams full of software engineers. “We see a lot of adoption being driven by data analysts, marketing teams, researchers, etc., within organizations,” says Darren Meyer, staff research engineer at Endor Labs.

These teams aren’t traditionally developing their own software but are increasingly writing simple tools that adopt AI libraries and models, so they’re often not aware of the risks involved. “This combination of shadow engineering with lower-than-average application security awareness can be a breeding ground for risk,” he adds.

To make sure these teams are working safely, CISOs must consider forming relationships with these teams early in the process. Cybersecurity leaders might also want to set up training programs tailored to non-traditional development teams to educate data analysts, marketing professionals, and researchers on the potential risks associated with AI-based tools and libraries.

Investing in defense

“Security budgets don’t generally grow at the same pace that software development accelerates, and AI adoption is only widening that gap,” Meyer says. Application security is often underfunded in most organizations, yet allocating sufficient time and resources to it is essential, as AI adoption and AI-assisted coding accelerate the pace of software development.

“A portfolio of high-quality security tools that can help address this gap is no longer optional,” Meyer says. “And while tools are critical to closing the gap, so are AppSec and ProdSec staff that can effectively partner with developers — even non-traditional developers — and understand the technical, compliance, and security implications of AI.”

When it comes to securing enough resources to protect AI systems, some stakeholders might hesitate, viewing it as an optional expense rather than a critical investment. “AI adoption is a divisive topic in many organizations, with some leaders and teams being ‘all-in’ on adoption and some being strongly resistant,” Meyer says. “This tension can present challenges for insightful CISOs and business information security officers (BISOs).”

CISOs that are aware of both the advantages and disadvantages of this might try to set controls to manage risks effectively, but this might create the perception of holding the organization back from innovating if they don’t explain what they do properly. “Organizations need to develop comprehensive strategies that balance the productivity benefits of AI tools with robust security practices,” says Thomas Segura, senior technical writer at GitGuardian.

Cost-effective changes CISOs should implement

But if a security leader has 90 days and no budget to spare, which changes would have the biggest impact?

Datadog’s Lankford says a short, plain-language AI tool policy can make expectations clear. At a minimum, such a policy should spell out which tools employees can use, what code and data they can share, and which changes need specialist review. The aim is to give people answers they can use while they work, with a clear point of contact when they’re unsure.

It’s also important to understand that employees don’t want to circumvent policies. They just want to get their work done without friction and without waiting weeks for approval. Giving them the right tools makes the safer route easier to take.

By contrast, banning tools doesn’t work, because employees will find a way to still use them. A ban can push AI use out of sight, leaving security teams with less visibility into the code being written and the data being shared, Mimecast’s Nielsen says.

CISOs should look across the development process to identify where they can intervene and which risks they can address at each stage. “Understand what layers you can influence and what vulnerabilities you can influence at each layer: in the design phase, in the CLAUDE.md file, as the agent is writing, during a pull request, as part of an AI pentest,” Semgrep’s Paxton-Fead says.

It’s also important to explain to employees who are using AI code-generating tools that security lives in an implicit context: the threat model, the trust boundaries, what the attacker controls. “Agents cannot reliably plan and reason on these, so they optimize for the only signal they have, which is to satisfy the given functionality description,” Carnegie Mellon’s Wang says.

When things go wrong, people in the organization need to feel safe telling security what happened, including which unapproved tools they used and what data they shared. Fear of punishment can delay that conversation, leaving the team trying to contain a problem without the full picture.

“Offer amnesty instead of a crackdown, so people tell you the truth about what they’re using,” Nielsen advises.

item.title: The resilience gap: Why cybersecurity investment alone is not enough
item.description:
Death, taxes and cyber incidents. It’s not quite the original saying, but for today’s CISO, all three carry a certain inevitability, and most organizations have come to accept that reality.

Protiviti’s 2027 CISO Top Risks and Opportunities study confirms that cybersecurity remains the top investment priority for CISOs. Yet even well-funded security programs can struggle when something goes wrong.

Why? The cause is rarely missing plans or controls; it’s silos. Service owners; security, recovery and crisis teams; and key providers too often plan and operate apart. As a result, organizations are beginning to see that investment and resilience are not the same thing.

Ultimately, the investment didn’t fail; the expectation did. Technology alone can’t deliver an outcome that also depends on people, process, governance and coordination. The lesson is clear: A well-funded cybersecurity program can still be operationally fragile.

The findings in Protiviti’s 2027 CISO Top Risks and Opportunities study illustrate the problem. Cybersecurity remains the leading strategic investment priority, selected by 48% of CISOs. Yet only 41% report high or very high confidence in their organizations’ ability to protect enterprise value, while just 29% express that level of confidence in responding with agility. Another 54% describe their confidence in their organizations’ ability to respond with agility as moderate.

That gap should concern every CISO. It suggests organizations have built security capabilities without fully developing the enterprise operating model needed during disruption.

The real test begins when prevention ends

Security investment matters. But you aren’t buying away cyber risk. You’re buying it down. Even the most mature organizations will eventually face an event they cannot prevent, often involving a third party, technology failure or circumstance outside their control.

What happens next separates resilient organizations from everyone else. Security works to contain the threat while infrastructure and application teams decide what can safely go offline. Business leaders push to restore critical services, sometimes with competing priorities. Legal weighs disclosure obligations with incomplete information. Communications prepares messages for employees, customers and regulators.

Meanwhile, a cloud, software-as-a-service or other technology provider may control part of the environment the company needs to recover.

That’s where resilience usually breaks down: not within any one team, but in the handoffs and decisions between them. In the exercises we run, the hardest questions are often surprisingly basic:

  • Who has the authority to shut down a revenue-producing system?
  • If two critical services are down, who decides which comes back first?
  • If Microsoft 365 or another primary collaboration platform is unavailable, how does the crisis team communicate?
  • If a critical provider is also down, do its recovery priorities and timelines align with yours?

The useful output of an exercise is not a reassuring score. It is the list of things that didn’t work: unclear authority, gaps in escalation paths, inaccessible backups and dependencies that teams incorrectly assumed had been tested. Consider Quantum Dawn VIII, SIFMA’s sector-wide exercise from November 2025. The polycrisis scenario included an undersea cable cut, and roughly two-thirds of participants said they had either never tested that scenario or weren’t sure they had. That is exactly the kind of blind spot an exercise is designed to expose. Better to uncover it in an exercise than during an actual disruption.

And the event you plan for is seldom the event you get. That’s why resilience cannot depend on following a script. Build a framework that enables collaboration and increases the speed of informed decisions, regardless of what actually happens.

Cyber, AI and third-party risks no longer stay in their lanes

Risks don’t arrive one at a time. A cyberattack can quickly become a privacy issue, a regulatory matter and a business interruption. A third-party outage becomes your outage. And AI can act as a force multiplier, allowing a single issue to move faster and spread across more data, systems and business processes.

The findings support this. Cyber threats remain the highest-rated near-term concern in the Top Risks survey, but privacy, third-party risk, AI, resilience and regulatory uncertainty are now clustered closely behind.

AI doesn’t change the fundamental resilience questions. It raises the stakes. An agent may read customer data, query an ERP system, act through a service account or trigger a workflow without a person clicking the button. So, start with an old question: What can it access? Then ask whose permissions or delegated authority it is using, what actions it can take, where those actions are logged and how quickly you can stop it when something goes wrong.

CISOs appear to recognize that challenge. In our 2027 Top Risks study, 51% identified improving AI governance and accountability as a leading priority, while 45% pointed to workforce readiness. That’s telling. Sustainable adoption requires some basic discipline: maintain an inventory of agents and their owners, map the data and tools each can reach, restrict service accounts and delegated permissions, monitor actions and make sure access can be revoked quickly.

Third parties deserve the same scrutiny. A third-party assessment can tell you a lot about a provider’s controls at a point in time. What it rarely tells you is how that provider will perform on a bad day. Most assessments still rely heavily on documentation, discussion and self-reporting. Those assessments may assure a provider’s security posture, but they do not prove that a critical service will remain available, that the provider’s recovery sequence aligns with yours or that the appropriate people on both sides know how to disconnect, communicate and restore service together.

CISOs should be able to identify the external relationships most critical to business operations, understand the services and data that depend on them, and test what will happen if those relationships are interrupted.

This broader responsibility is increasingly part of the CISO mandate. CSO’s examination of how CISOs can rise to the business resilience challenge describes the role’s evolution from a primarily preventive function toward greater responsibility for response, recovery and business resilience.

Build resilience into the investments already underway

If cyber risk increasingly travels through interconnected systems and infrastructure, resilience has to be part of how those environments are modernized in the first place.

The percentage of CISOs selecting cybersecurity slipped from 53% to 48%, while the percentage selecting infrastructure modernization rose from 21% to 33%. Taken together, those shifts make sense. Security and modernization are increasingly intertwined. A cloud migration, enterprise resource planning (ERP) replacement, identity redesign or data-platform upgrade can retire unsupported systems and standing privileges. It can also create new concentration risk, recovery dependencies and failure points if resilience is not designed in from the start.

CISOs should use these major transformation programs to improve resilience, not complicate it. Questions to ask include:

  • Are we retiring legacy platforms and connections, or simply putting a new layer on top of them?
  • Are old accounts, interfaces, backup jobs and vendor dependencies actually being removed?
  • Can the order-to-cash, payments, customer service or other critical processes be restored faster after the investment?
  • Are recovery, isolation and alternate-processing requirements in the architecture and acceptance criteria from the start?
  • Have we tested the new platform’s recovery path, or are we assuming modernization made it more resilient?

Closing the resilience gap

The point isn’t to spend less on cybersecurity. It’s to expect more from the investment. The 2027 Top Risks study shows CISOs balancing cyber threats with AI, third-party risk, resilience and modernization. Those may look like separate priorities on a survey. In practice, they increasingly collide in the same incident.

We aren’t going to prevent every cyber incident. The question is what happens when the next one gets through. Does the organization know what matters most, who makes the hard calls and how to recover? Or does it figure those things out during the crisis?

That gap is the resilience gap. And it is where CISOs should be looking next.
